rationale: This is a cosmetic re-shuffling of CleanGrowthVersusFragileBloat — identical long corner, with the short corner's two ingredients swapped for other already-tested archive components (level-bloat from IndNeutralOperatingCapitalBloatDecay, loss-frequency from AccrualBuildupWeakProfitRecord) — so it recycles the same information set rather than introducing a new mechanism.

The three conjuncts are economically sequential rather than redundant and the sign is internally consistent (all legs increase with impairment risk, product high = bad, expected negative), though it is an incremental short-side mirror of the already-tested triple conjunction and risks thinning the extreme portfolio into an illiquid distressed corner rather than sharpening it.

Change in total liabilities scaled by assets is a well-known external-financing/asset-growth anomaly component and is mechanically correlated with the working-capital accrual leg (both are pieces of balance-sheet growth), so the composite is close to a repackaged asset-growth × accrual sort and also a sign-mirror of the already-tested DebtFinancedAccrualBuildup.

The conservatism direction is genuinely untested here and the sign matches the expression, but dpc/sale is largely the inverse of asset turnover even within industry — precisely the variable the archive finds predicts *negatively* — so the conditioner may load on capital intensity/low turnover and fight the hypothesized sign.

RE/BE is a recognized lifecycle/quality proxy rather than a novel construct and is unstable for near-zero or negative book equity, but its pairing with a contemporaneous clean-accrual leg is a legitimately new, low-noise conditioner; note the stated mechanism (mature self-funded firms with *rising* working capital) describes a mid-range corner of the product, not its short leg.

This is the double sign-flip of IndNeutralOperatingCapitalBloatDecay — since IND_RANK(NEG(x)) ≈ 1 − IND_RANK(x), the signal equals 1 − a − b + ab against the tested ab — so it differs only by a linear rank term and is too near-mechanical a variant to count as a distinct stock-versus-flow test.
